text: You already understand software supply chain risk: a project pulls in open-source packages it didn't write, and a compromised dependency becomes a compromised application. Modern machine learning works the same way. Almost nobody trains a large model from zero anymore — teams pull a pretrained model from a hub like Hugging Face, fine-tune it, and ship it. That model, and the dataset it was built from, are third-party dependencies carrying exactly the same category of risk as an npm package or a PyPI wheel.

The difference is that the ML ecosystem's supply chain tooling is far less mature than software's. There's no widely adopted SBOM equivalent for models yet — what exists instead are model cards and dataset cards, publisher-written documentation describing training data, intended use, and known limitations. They're genuinely useful, but they're self-reported, not independently verified the way a signed package checksum is. And the same risk applies to datasets: a web-scraped corpus inherits whatever mislabeled or low-quality content existed in its source material, because nobody manually reviewed billions of examples.

Here's a real, documented risk worth knowing by name. Older PyTorch checkpoints were commonly saved using Python's pickle format, which has a well-known design flaw: it can execute arbitrary code during deserialization. That means simply loading a malicious checkpoint file — not running it, just loading it — can execute attacker-controlled code on your machine. That's exactly why Hugging Face now promotes safetensors as the default checkpoint format: it stores only tensor data, with nothing executable in the load path, closing that risk off entirely.

So what do you actually check before loading something you didn't build? Favor safetensors over a pickle-only release, and treat a pickle-only model as a reason to look closer rather than an automatic red flag. Check the publisher's reputation the same way you'd check a package maintainer — official accounts, download history, community review carry real signal. Pin and hash-verify the weights and dataset files you depend on, and run the hub's own scanning tools as a first filter, never as a substitute for your own review. Watch for typosquatting on model and dataset names too — the same risk npm and PyPI already face.

Once you've vetted what you're loading, the next question is what happens when that trust is misused deliberately. Lesson 11 looks at backdoor attacks — the most structured, hardest-to-catch version of the targeted poisoning from Lesson 9 — and the real detection techniques researchers built specifically because ordinary accuracy testing doesn't surface them.
